faqs.question: Can I give someone marigolds as a gift in India?
faqs.answer: It depends entirely on the family and the region, not on the flower. A 2021 Tamil Nadu Agricultural University survey records marigold garlands at Telugu weddings and on Lord Shiva at Shivaratri, and also on the dead in Tamil and Malayali burial rites. If you do not know the household's practice, ask before you buy.

faqs.question: What does genda phool mean in English?
faqs.answer: Genda phool simply means marigold flower. Genda or gainda is the Hindi name for Tagetes erecta, the large African or Mexican marigold, and phool means flower. The same plant is zendu in Marathi, banthi in Telugu and samanthi or chendu malli in Tamil.

faqs.question: Is it rude to bring marigolds to someone's home?
faqs.answer: No documented rule found in these sources says so. The same Tamil Nadu survey records marigold used at a house-warming puja and at Valaikappu, the seventh-month baby shower. Because usage varies by community, a quick question to the host is more reliable than any general rule.

faqs.question: Which marigold species is grown in India?
faqs.answer: Mostly Tagetes erecta, the large-flowered African or Mexican marigold, with the smaller Tagetes patula also grown. Indian agronomy work uses cultivars such as Pusa Narangi Gainda, and the loose-flower trade is dominated by the African types because they string into garlands more easily.

faqs.question: Why are marigold garlands cheaper than rose garlands?
faqs.answer: Volume and durability. A 2015 value-chain case study from Tamil Nadu reports one grower's marigold yield at 4–5 tonnes per acre with a pre-intervention farm-gate price of ₹2–3 per kilogram. Marigold also tolerates handling better, which cuts the losses a seller has to price in.

faqs.question: Does the colour of a marigold change what it means?
faqs.answer: None of the sources cited here assign different meanings to orange and yellow marigold in Hindu practice. What the field surveys record is the flower being chosen by role and occasion rather than by shade, so colour claims about Indian marigold should be treated with caution.

faqs.question: How many blooms does the SubhSandesh bouquet builder offer?
faqs.answer: Twelve: orchid, tulip, dahlia, anemone, carnation, zinnia, ranunculus, sunflower, lily, daisy, peony and rose. It is a fixed set, so marigold cannot be added to a bouquet on the page. The digital bouquet is SubhSandesh's #2 page type at 796 created, 23.4% of all pages.

faqs.question: What happens to flowers after they are offered at a temple?
faqs.answer: Often they become waste. A 2025 case study of Kannauj district in Uttar Pradesh reports three temples there disposing of several quintals of offered flowers between them daily, and examines converting that material into itra rather than dumping it in water bodies or open pits.

faqs.question: Is marigold originally from India?
faqs.answer: No. Horticultural reference works list Tagetes erecta as the African or Mexican marigold, and the genus is not Indian in origin. Its central place in Indian ritual floristry was acquired rather than inherited, which is one reason older Sanskrit flower lists are not a reliable guide to it.

faqs.question: Should I ask a family before choosing marigold for their occasion?
faqs.answer: Yes, and that is the practical conclusion of the evidence rather than a hedge. Within one state, one survey found marigold garlands reserved for corpses in one community and used on a bride and groom in another. The family's own practice is the only reliable authority.

faqs.question: How long do marigolds keep compared with roses?
faqs.answer: Marigold holds up noticeably better. The 2025 ICAR review classes it as only moderately ethylene-sensitive where rose and jasmine are highly sensitive, and gives its optimal storage temperature as 8–12°C against 0–2°C for rose. That tolerance is why it survives an unrefrigerated cart.

# Marigold Flower Meaning in Hinduism, From Documented Practice

There is no single marigold flower meaning in Hinduism. It is the everyday flower of devotion at scale, and what it signifies shifts with region and community rather than with the bloom itself. Agricultural researchers at ICAR record 2,284,000 tonnes of loose flowers grown in India in 2023–24 against 947,000 tonnes of cut flowers, and marigold takes the largest single share of that loose-flower crop. On SubhSandesh the digital bouquet is the #2 page type — 796 created, 23.4% of all pages — out of 3,397 personalised pages built across 15 page types since 2026-03-12. Marigold is not among the twelve blooms that builder offers, which is the honest limit of what this page can hand you. What follows comes from field surveys and floriculture data rather than a symbolism chart: the flower's names, its volumes, four documented uses, and the point where the evidence stops.

## What is the marigold in Hindu worship?

The marigold in Indian worship is a cheap, sturdy, year-round flower used loose or strung, offered to deities and hung on doorways, images, vehicles and biers. Botanically it is *Tagetes erecta*, listed in horticultural reference works as the African or Mexican marigold, alongside the smaller-flowered *Tagetes patula*. In everyday speech it is *genda* or *gainda* in Hindi, *zendu* in Marathi, *banthi* in Telugu, and *samanthi* or *chendu malli* in Tamil. Indian agronomy carries the vernacular straight through — Pusa Narangi Gainda is a standard African marigold variety in the research literature.

English-language flower symbolism usually glosses marigold as warmth, creativity or the sun. That reading is not wrong; it is simply beside the point here, because in Indian practice the flower's meaning is set by what people do with it rather than by an assigned sentiment. The rest of this page follows the doing.

## Marigold is India's ritual flower by volume, not by symbolism

The strongest claim available about marigold in Hindu practice is a quantitative one. A 2025 review in the *Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences* by ICAR-Indian Agricultural Research Institute scientists defines "traditional flowers" as species grown for religious, cultural and ceremonial use, mostly in loose form, and [names marigold first among them](https://epubs.icar.org.in/index.php/IJAgS/article/view/156841) alongside jasmine, chrysanthemum and rose.

The scale is lopsided in a way most flower writing misses. As of 2023–24, India's floriculture covered 285,000 hectares and produced 2,284,000 tonnes of loose flowers against 947,000 tonnes of cut flowers — roughly 2.4 tonnes of ritual flower for every tonne of bouquet flower. A doctoral study of loose-flower production and use in Tamil Nadu puts [marigold at more than half of the national loose-flower crop](https://shodhganga.inflibnet.ac.in/handle/10603/463557) on its own, and records 1,779 hectares of it inside Tamil Nadu producing 31,777 tonnes.

That volume leaves a trail. A 2025 case study of Kannauj district in Uttar Pradesh reports that three temples there — Sheetala Chaukiya, Diyawan Mahadev and Markandeya Mahadev — [dispose of several quintals of offered flowers between them every day](https://www.sagens.org/journal/agens/article/view/s2025030107), which is the physical residue of the practice this article is about.

## Four uses recorded in one field survey

The most useful evidence on what marigold means is not a symbolism list but one survey that asked people what they actually do. J. I. Jergin's 2021 thesis at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University documented loose-flower use across the state's linguistic and religious groups, and marigold turns up in four quite different roles inside it.

### 1. Garlanding a deity at Shivaratri

The practice: garlands of marigold, tulsi and rose used to decorate Lord Shiva, and the temple elephants alongside him, at Shivaratri. Recorded among Malayali respondents in the survey's Kanyakumari, Tirunelveli, Coimbatore, Nilgiris and Theni settlements. The same study records a temple function called Koodalumooduthooku celebrated with nerium, marigold and paneer rose, garlands woven over nochi and bulrush leaf. This is marigold at its most straightforwardly auspicious — on the deity, at one of the year's larger Shaiva observances.

### 2. Wedding garlands in Telugu practice

The practice: three garlands at a wedding, made of chrysanthemum, tuberose and marigold. Recorded among Telugu-speaking families settled in Chennai, Coimbatore, Tiruvallur, Kanchipuram, Krishnagiri, Tiruvannamalai and Vellore. The same group is recorded using nerium, chrysanthemum and marigold at Ugadi and Bhogi. Marigold is a wedding flower here — in the same state where, as the next entries show, other communities keep it well away from a wedding.

### 3. Harvest festivals and cattle

The practice: floral carpets, *poo kolam*, laid at Pongal from paneer rose, marigold and chrysanthemum. Recorded among Tamil respondents, for the festival held on the first day of the Tamil month of Thai. On the third day, Mattu Pongal, cattle are bathed, their horns painted, and they are garlanded with marigold, cock's comb and chrysanthemum. Marigold also appears in the survey at Valaikappu, the seventh-month baby shower, where the expectant mother is garlanded with tuberose, marigold and rose.

### 4. Funeral garlands and scattered petals

The practice: garlanding the dead, and scattering loose petals along the funeral route. Recorded among both Tamil and Malayali respondents. The Tamil wording in the thesis is blunt — marigold and Nityakalyani garlands "are used only for corpses in burial rituals". Malayali respondents garland their dead with marigold and rose, and loose petals of paneer rose, marigold and chrysanthemum are spread on the street during the procession.

## Why "marigold is a funeral flower in India" collapses on contact with the record

This is the claim to handle carefully, because it is half true and usually stated as though it were whole. Marigold's funerary use is real and documented. So is its use on a deity, at a wedding, at a harvest festival and around a pregnancy — in the same survey, the same state, the same year.

The sharpest line in Jergin's thesis, that marigold garlands are used only for corpses, describes what Tamil respondents reported. A few pages later the same thesis has Telugu-speaking families in Tamil Nadu putting a marigold garland on a bride and groom. Both statements are accurate. Neither is a national rule, and treating either as one is how a gift goes wrong.

A second study points the same way. Fieldwork on the Kinnaura community's Fulaich festival in Kinnaur, Himachal Pradesh, [published in the *Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge* in July 2024](https://or.niscpr.res.in/index.php/IJTK/article/view/1348), describes one festival, running from 10 August to 26 October, whose stated purposes include offering high-altitude wild flowers to local deities, paying homage to departed family members, and celebrating a new birth. Honouring the dead and welcoming a birth are not separate floral registers there. They are the same festival, with 47 plant species recorded across it.

So the practical answer is unglamorous: for a specific family in a specific place, ask that family. Nothing in these sources supports a pan-Indian marigold taboo, and no source found here documents a deity-specific prohibition on marigold, so this page does not assert one.

## What marigold means spiritually, and what it cannot be made to say

Asked what marigold means spiritually, the part that can be answered honestly is functional. It is the flower of offering at scale: available almost year-round, strung into a garland fast, and tough enough to survive a day on an image, a bonnet or a doorframe.

That toughness is measurable. The ICAR review classes marigold as only moderately ethylene-sensitive, where rose, jasmine, tuberose and carnation are highly sensitive, and puts its optimal storage temperature at 8–12°C against 0–2°C for rose and chrysanthemum. It also estimates post-harvest losses of India's traditional flowers at 30–40%. A flower that tolerates a warm cart through a morning is the flower that ends up in daily worship, and that is closer to an explanation than any assigned sentiment.

The farm economics run in the same direction. A 2015 NAIP value-chain case study from Tamil Nadu Agricultural University reports [one grower's marigold yield falling to 4–5 tonnes per acre](http://researchjournal.co.in/online/IJCBM/IJCBM%208%281%29/8_112-116_A.pdf) and a pre-intervention farm-gate price of ₹2–3 per kilogram; only that paper's abstract is readable, so that is all it is cited for. Ritual flowers are bought by weight, and marigold fills a garland more cheaply than anything else.

What the sources will not support is a scriptural gloss. No citable text found here assigns marigold a fixed doctrinal meaning, and none of these surveys frames it that way.

## Marigold beside the blooms a digital bouquet can send

This table sets five traditional Indian flowers against their post-harvest behaviour in the ICAR review and against whether SubhSandesh's bouquet builder actually carries them.

| Flower | Ethylene sensitivity (ICAR, 2025) | Optimal storage (°C) | In SubhSandesh's 12-bloom set? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marigold (*Tagetes erecta*) | Moderate | 8–12 | No |
| Rose | High | 0–2 | Yes |
| Jasmine | High | 4–7 | No |
| Chrysanthemum | Moderate | 0–2 | No |
| Carnation | High | 0–2 | Yes |

The takeaway is awkward and worth stating plainly: the flower carrying the heaviest documented ritual load is the one the builder does not offer. Rose and carnation are among the twelve; orchid, tulip, dahlia, anemone, zinnia, ranunculus, sunflower, lily, daisy and peony fill the rest. If you want marigold, the [build-a-bouquet page](https://subhsandesh.in/bouquet-gf) cannot give it to you.

## When sending a page is the wrong answer

Three cases where SubhSandesh loses outright. The first is an offering: a puja needs a physical flower in a physical hand, and nothing rendered on a screen substitutes for one. The second is marigold itself — absent from the twelve blooms, so a page cannot show the flower this article is about.

The third is the device. 50.2% of shared pages are opened on a phone, 20,937 of 41,682 recorded views, which is a coin flip rather than a guarantee; a recipient on a feature phone or a locked-down office desktop is a poor fit. Where the message is romantic rather than ritual, the [romantic "I love you" page](https://subhsandesh.in/love-gf) or the [darker, more dramatic Darling page](https://subhsandesh.in/darling) carry the intent better than a bouquet whose symbolism you are still deciding.

## Sources

- Jain R. and others, "Preservation of freshness in flowers", *Indian Journal of Agricultural Sciences* 95(10): 1147–1155, October 2025.
- Jergin J. I., "An explorative study on production and uses of loose flowers in Tamil Nadu", doctoral thesis, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, 2021.
- Lata S. and others, "Festival of flowers (Fulaich)", *Indian Journal of Traditional Knowledge* 23(7), 16 July 2024.
- Shukla P. and Ali M., "Utilizing temple floral waste to address the resource crunch in the perfume industry: Kannauj district", *AgroEnvironmental Sustainability* 3(1), 15 March 2025.
- Ravikumar R. and Rajesh A., "Success of marigold farming: an intervention by NAIP", *International Journal of Commerce and Business Management* 8(1): 112–116, 15 April 2015. Abstract only.

auditReport.honestAssessment: The nine sites holding the bare 'marigold flower meaning' SERP — petalrepublic, florgeous, flowermeaning.com, bloomingexpert, myglobalflowers, floristempire, theflowerexpert, foliagefriend and floweraura — all answer the query as US/UK flower symbolism, and none of them can print what this post prints: a named 2021 TNAU doctoral survey in which marigold garlands a corpse in one Tamil community, a bride in a Telugu community in the same state, and Lord Shiva among Malayali respondents, plus ICAR's 2025 loose-versus-cut-flower tonnage. That is a genuine, sourceable body of material they do not cover, and it is the reason an answer engine would cite this for the Hinduism variant. It is not enough to take the head term: those nine are topically dedicated domains with far more authority and backlinks, and Indian-first framing does not close an authority gap — what would change the picture is external links from Indian horticulture, temple or festival sites, and a second and third post building a real marigold/ritual-flower cluster rather than one page. Ranking takes months and is not predicted here. UNVERIFIED CLAIMS DELIBERATELY LEFT OUT, by body line: (1) that marigold reads as a funeral flower across India — the orchestrator's earlier brief asserted this and it is contradicted by the wedding and Shivaratri uses in the very same survey, so the post says the opposite in the section 'Why "marigold is a funeral flower in India" collapses on contact with the record'; (2) any deity-specific prohibition on offering marigold — searched and not found, and the same section states explicitly that no source found here documents one; (3) any scriptural or Sanskrit-text meaning for marigold — stated as absent in 'What marigold means spiritually, and what it cannot be made to say' rather than invented; (4) colour-specific meanings for orange versus yellow marigold in Hindu practice — omitted from the body and answered as 'not found' in the FAQ 'Does the colour of a marigold change what it means?'; (5) the history and date of Tagetes's introduction to India — the body says only that reference works list it as the African or Mexican marigold and the FAQ 'Is marigold originally from India?' claims no more than that, because no dated source for the introduction was verified; (6) the vernacular name list (genda, gainda, zendu, banthi, samanthi, chendu malli) and the cultivar name Pusa Narangi Gainda are given without a citation — the names appear across the Indian agronomy literature seen during research, including Shodhganga thesis titles, but no single source was fetched that lists them together, so no link is attached to that sentence; (7) marigold's national area and production in hectares and tonnes — no reachable government horticulture table was retrieved (nhb.gov.in state files 404, agriwelfare.gov.in returned 403), so only the Tamil Nadu figures and the 'more than half of national loose-flower production' share are stated. Two intended sources were surrendered rather than reused or laundered: the Ethnobotany Research and Applications Kullu magico-religious survey, which documents Tagetes decorating deities' palanquins and would have been the single best ritual citation, is already spent in USED-SOURCES.md at ethnobotanyjournal.org/index.php/era/article/view/4535; and the MDPI Horticulturae marigold-productivity paper from Jammu (10.3390/horticulturae8030263) was verified open-access but mdpi.com, nbn-resolving.org and every mirror bot-blocked every fetch, so it is not cited.
